Model 1: Variable Selection Across the Full Candidate Set

Section 5.4 implemented in nine reviewable steps

Author

Analysis Team

Published

July 29, 2026

Mission

Model 0 rehearsed the LASSO machinery on one Andersen domain and returned a usable but narrow verdict. Model 1 executes Section 5.4 as written: the full candidate set, the primary outcome, and all four model specifications.

The proposal asks for four LASSO fits and a negative binomial refit of each. It does not say which candidates survive contact with the data, what to do when a variable is missing by survey design rather than by non-response, or how to reconcile a pooled two-cycle sample with predictors that only one province answered. Those questions are settled here, and every settlement is recorded.

This report is built to be vetted, not merely read. It is organised as nine steps. Each step produces artifacts a reviewer can check independently, and each closes with a review point naming exactly what a reader should agree or disagree with before the next step is allowed to stand. A reader who rejects a review point can stop there: everything downstream inherits it.

What this report is not

Model 1 is a selection report. It answers “which variables belong in the model,” not “what is the effect of chronic conditions on absenteeism.” The rate ratios in Step 8 are conditional on a selection procedure that used the same data, so their confidence intervals are optimistic. They are shown to demonstrate that the two-stage handoff works and to let a reviewer sanity-check direction and magnitude, not as estimates for publication.

Research questions:

  1. Which of the 50 registered candidate variables are eligible for selection at all, and on what evidence are the ineligible ones excluded?
  2. What analytic sample survives, and does surviving it distort the sample?
  3. What does each of the four specifications retain?
  4. Do the retained sets match the counts the proposal anticipates (16, 9, 32, 33)?
  5. Does the two-stage Poisson-to-negative-binomial handoff hold at full scale?

Definition of Terms

Candidate registry. The single table naming every variable eligible for selection, its Andersen domain, and — where it is excluded — the reason. Earlier exploratory work kept these lists in several places and they drifted. Step 1 replaces them with one object that every later step reads from.

Design column. After reference-cell dummy coding, a factor with \(k\) levels becomes \(k-1\) columns. LASSO penalizes columns; the proposal counts variables. A variable is retained here when at least one of its columns survives.

lambda.min / lambda.1se. The penalty minimizing cross-validated deviance, and the largest penalty whose deviance remains within one standard error of that minimum. The latter buys parsimony at a cost in fit that cross-validation cannot distinguish from noise.

Forced variable. A column exempted from the penalty via penalty.factor = 0, so it cannot be selected out. The cycle indicator is forced: a pooled sample requires it whether or not it earns its place.

Missing by design. An answer absent because the question was never asked — because of a skip pattern, or because the content was optional and a province declined it. Distinct from non-response, and it must be treated differently: imputing a value for a question nobody was asked invents data.

Structural alias. A variable whose missingness pattern is a near-perfect function of another variable already in the model. Including it lets the model learn the design of the survey instead of the biology of the respondent.

# The three self-perceived measures that Section 5.4 toggles on and off.

Helpers for design construction, penalised fitting, and negative binomial refitting 
# Render a data frame as styled HTML for Quarto, or plainly for console use.
# Tall tables get a fixed-height scroll box so the report stays navigable.
print_table <- function(data, caption, align = NULL, scroll_height = NULL) {
  if (is.null(scroll_height) && nrow(data) > 25) scroll_height <- "600px"
  boxed <- data %>%
    knitr::kable(
      format = "html", caption = caption, escape = FALSE,
      align = align, row.names = FALSE
    ) %>%
    kableExtra::kable_styling(
      bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE
    )
  boxed <- if (is.null(scroll_height)) {
    kableExtra::scroll_box(boxed, width = "100%")
  } else {
    kableExtra::scroll_box(boxed, width = "100%", height = scroll_height)
  }
  cat(as.character(boxed))
  invisible(data)
}

to_yes_no <- function(x) {
  factor(ifelse(x %in% c(1, TRUE), "Yes", "No"), levels = c("No", "Yes"))
}

# Strip the variable-name prefix from a design column to recover the level
# label. Vectorised, because sub() uses only the first element of `pattern`.
strip_variable_prefix <- function(column, variable) {
  purrr::map2_chr(column, variable, ~ sub(paste0("^", .y), "", .x))
}

# Build a design matrix and the column-to-variable map that makes selection
# results interpretable. Reference contrasts; intercept dropped.
build_design <- function(model_frame, term_vars) {
  model_formula <- stats::reformulate(term_vars)
  mm <- stats::model.matrix(model_formula, data = model_frame)
  assign_index <- attr(mm, "assign")
  term_labels <- attr(stats::terms(model_formula, data = model_frame), "term.labels")
  source_variable <- c("(Intercept)", term_labels)[assign_index + 1]
  keep <- colnames(mm) != "(Intercept)"

  list(
    x = mm[, keep, drop = FALSE],
    map = tibble::tibble(
      column = colnames(mm)[keep],
      variable = source_variable[keep]
    ) %>%
      mutate(level = strip_variable_prefix(column, variable))
  )
}

# Stage 1. A weighted, L1-penalised Poisson fit with the cycle indicator exempt
# from the penalty, plus the full coefficient path for plotting.
fit_lasso <- function(design, outcome, weights, seed) {
  penalty_vector <- as.numeric(!design$map$variable %in% forced_vars)

  set.seed(seed)
  path <- glmnet::glmnet(
    x = design$x, y = outcome, family = "poisson", alpha = 1,
    weights = weights, penalty.factor = penalty_vector
  )
  set.seed(seed)
  cv <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(
    x = design$x, y = outcome, family = "poisson", alpha = 1,
    nfolds = lasso_folds, weights = weights, penalty.factor = penalty_vector
  )
  list(path = path, cv = cv, penalty = penalty_vector)
}

# Extract the coefficient vector at a named lambda, joined to the column map.
coefficients_at <- function(lasso, design, lambda_rule) {
  coefficient_matrix <- stats::coef(lasso$cv, s = lambda_rule)
  tibble::tibble(
    column = rownames(coefficient_matrix),
    estimate = as.numeric(coefficient_matrix)
  ) %>%
    filter(column != "(Intercept)") %>%
    left_join(design$map, by = "column") %>%
    mutate(retained = estimate != 0)
}

# Decision 9: a variable is promoted to stage 2 if ANY of its columns survived.
retained_variables <- function(coefficient_table) {
  coefficient_table %>%
    filter(retained) %>%
    pull(variable) %>%
    unique()
}

# Stage 2. Unpenalised negative binomial on the retained variable set.
fit_nb <- function(model_frame, term_vars, outcome) {
  terms_used <- if (length(term_vars) > 0) term_vars else "1"
  model_formula <- stats::reformulate(terms_used, response = outcome)
  environment(model_formula) <- environment()
  suppressWarnings(
    MASS::glm.nb(
      model_formula, data = model_frame, weights = weight_scaled,
      control = stats::glm.control(maxit = 50)
    )
  )
}

# Wald summary on the rate-ratio scale. NOT bootstrap: see decision 10.
tidy_nb <- function(nb_fit, column_map) {
  summary(nb_fit)$coefficients %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("column") %>%
    rename(estimate = Estimate, std_error = `Std. Error`, p_value = `Pr(>|z|)`) %>%
    filter(column != "(Intercept)") %>%
    left_join(column_map, by = "column") %>%
    mutate(
      rate_ratio = exp(estimate),
      ci_low = exp(estimate - 1.96 * std_error),
      ci_high = exp(estimate + 1.96 * std_error)
    )
}

Build the model frame, apply complete-case filtering, and construct both design matrices 
# Decision 5: complete-case on the included candidate set only. Excluding
# cc_copd and has_family_doctor first (decisions 2 and 3) is what makes a
# complete-case analysis tenable at all.
ds_model_raw <- ds0 %>%
  select(all_of(c(outcome_var, weight_col, cycle_var, included_vars))) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.ordered), ~ factor(., ordered = FALSE))) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.logical), to_yes_no)) %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(c("dhhgle5", "dhhg611", "dhhgl12")), to_yes_no)) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), factor))

n_source <- nrow(ds_model_raw)
complete_flag <- stats::complete.cases(ds_model_raw)

ds1 <- ds_model_raw %>%
  filter(complete_flag) %>%
  mutate(
    .respondent_id = dplyr::row_number(),
    weight_scaled = .data[[weight_col]] / mean(.data[[weight_col]])
  )

n_analytic <- nrow(ds1)

design_exclude <- build_design(ds1, c(forced_vars, vars_excluding_perceived))
design_include <- build_design(ds1, c(forced_vars, vars_including_perceived))
designs <- list(exclude = design_exclude, include = design_include)

y_outcome <- ds1[[outcome_var]]
weight_vector <- ds1$weight_scaled

variable_labels <- c(
  stats::setNames(candidate_registry$variable_label, candidate_registry$variable),
  stats::setNames("CCHS cycle", cycle_var)
)
variable_domains <- c(
  stats::setNames(candidate_registry$domain, candidate_registry$variable),
  stats::setNames("Survey design", cycle_var)
)

Reading the outcome summary

The variance-to-mean ratio is the number that governs the rest of the report. A Poisson likelihood assumes it equals 1. It does not, by a wide margin, which is why stage one uses Poisson only as a selection device — where the penalty dominates the likelihood — and stage two re-estimates under a negative binomial.

Analysis

Step 1 — The Candidate Registry

Section 5.4 says “all candidate predictors.” Establishing what that phrase denotes is the first substantive act of the analysis, and it is not a bookkeeping chore: two of the fifty registered variables turn out to be unusable, and finding that out is what makes the rest of the report possible.

Review point 1

Agree or disagree that the registry is complete and correctly domained. Three variables are marked excluded; the evidence for two of them is presented in Step 2 and should be judged there. The third, dhhgage, is excluded because age_group_3 already encodes age at the resolution Section 2.2 specifies, and offering both would give the penalty two versions of the same information.

Step 2 — Missing Data

The proposal’s Section 5.1 permits a “missing” category when the missing share is small. Two candidates are nowhere near small, and neither is missing for a reason that imputation or a missing-category would honestly represent.

Compute missingness by variable and cycle 
missingness_by_cycle <- ds0 %>%
  select(all_of(c(cycle_var, candidate_registry$variable))) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    -all_of(cycle_var), names_to = "variable", values_transform = as.character,
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  group_by(cycle = .data[[cycle_var]], variable) %>%
  summarise(pct_missing = 100 * mean(is.na(value)), .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(
    candidate_registry %>% select(variable, domain, variable_label, status),
    by = "variable"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    variable_label = forcats::fct_reorder(variable_label, pct_missing, .fun = max)
  )

complete_case_cascade <- tibble::tribble(
  ~scenario, ~variables_used,
  "All 50 candidates", candidate_registry$variable,
  "Drop cc_copd", setdiff(candidate_registry$variable, "cc_copd"),
  "Drop has_family_doctor", setdiff(candidate_registry$variable, "has_family_doctor"),
  "Drop both (chosen)", setdiff(candidate_registry$variable,
                                c("cc_copd", "has_family_doctor")),
  "Chosen set, minus dhhgage", included_vars
) %>%
  mutate(
    n_variables = lengths(variables_used),
    n_complete = purrr::map_int(variables_used,
                                ~ sum(stats::complete.cases(ds0[, .x]))),
    pct_retained = 100 * n_complete / nrow(ds0)
  )

readr::write_csv(
  missingness_by_cycle %>% mutate(variable_label = as.character(variable_label)),
  paste0(local_data, "missingness-by-cycle.csv")
)

Two points sit far to the right of everything else, and they are far to the right for different reasons.

Retaining it would encode cycle crossed with province, not health access.

The COPD question was administered only to respondents aged 35 and over: it is 100% missing below that age and essentially complete above it. A missing indicator for COPD would therefore be a re-labelled age indicator, and age_group_3 is already a candidate.

The family-doctor question is worse. In 2010–2011 it was optional content that only Ontario selected, so its missingness is an almost exact function of cycle crossed with province — both of which are in the model. Retaining it would let the penalty learn Statistics Canada’s content-selection process.

Table t2: Complete-case cascade. Excluding two structurally missing variables raises retention from 36.3% to 75.8%.
Scenario Variables Complete cases Retained (%)
All 50 candidates 51 23,152 36.3%
Drop cc_copd 50 32,395 50.7%
Drop has_family_doctor 50 34,261 53.7%
Drop both (chosen) 49 48,422 75.8%
Chosen set, minus dhhgage 48 48,422 75.8%

The cascade quantifies the price of each choice. Keeping both variables costs roughly two thirds of the sample; dropping both recovers about three quarters of it.

Review point 2

Agree or disagree that cc_copd and has_family_doctor should be excluded rather than imputed or given a missing category. If you disagree, the cascade table tells you what the alternative costs in sample size, and decisions 2 and 3 in Step 4 record how to reverse the choice.

Note the deferred alternative: COPD remains analysable in an age-35-and-over subsample, which is where Section 5.7’s condition-specific model for COPD would have to live in any case.

Complete-case analysis discards respondents, and discarding is only safe if the discarded resemble the retained. They do not have to match exactly — the model conditions on the variables shown — but a large divergence would signal that the estimates describe a population narrower than intended.

Agree or disagree that the analytic sample is close enough to the source population for complete-case analysis to stand. The comparison is descriptive, not a test; a formal treatment would require the multiple imputation Section 5.1 contemplates, which decision 5 defers.

Step 4 — The Decision Registry

Everything the proposal left open, and how each gap was closed. This table is the spine of the report’s reviewability: it names the alternatives that were available, the one taken, the reason, and whether the choice can be reversed.

Table t3: Decision registry. Every choice made between the Ellis table and the fitted models.
# Decision Alternatives considered Chosen Rationale Reverse by editing
1 Outcome variable days_absent_total; days_absent_chronic days_absent_total Section 5.5 designates it primary, and the 16/9/32/33 reproduction targets derive from it. outcome_var in declare-globals
2 COPD indicator Include; exclude; recode as No / Yes / Not asked Exclude Asked only of respondents aged 35+, so 100% missing below 35 and 30.9% missing in the 25-54 band. A ‘not asked’ level would be a deterministic function of age, which is already in the model. candidate_registry status for cc_copd
3 Family doctor indicator Include; exclude Exclude Optional content in 2010-2011, selected only by Ontario: 100% missing in every other province that cycle. Retaining it would make the variable a near-perfect alias for cycle crossed with province. candidate_registry status for has_family_doctor
4 Age resolution age_group_3; dhhgage; both age_group_3 The two encode the same construct and would compete arbitrarily under the penalty. Section 2.2 specifies the three-category recode. candidate_registry status for dhhgage
5 Missing data handling Complete case; explicit Missing level; multiple imputation Complete case After decisions 2 and 3 the loss falls from 63.7% to roughly 24%. Section 5.1 permits a separate category only below 5%, which several variables exceed; multiple imputation is deferred rather than dismissed. tweak-data-0 chunk
6 Perceived health definition The 3 self-perceived measures; the whole Needs domain The 3 self-perceived measures Ratified 2026-07-29. ADL items measure functional limitation, not perception, and injury status is a distinct construct. perceived_health_vars in declare-globals
7 Dummy coding scheme Reference (treatment) contrasts; full one-hot Reference contrasts Matches the stage-two negative binomial parameterisation. The snippet in Section 5.4 mixes both schemes and is internally inconsistent. build_design() in declare-functions
8 Cycle indicator Penalised; unpenalised Unpenalised (penalty.factor = 0) The pooled design requires a cycle term whether or not it survives selection. forced_vars in declare-globals
9 Carry-forward rule to stage 2 Any surviving column promotes the whole factor; retained levels only Any surviving column promotes the whole factor Preserves standard factor contrasts in the negative binomial refit. Level-wise carry-forward would produce non-standard contrasts that are hard to interpret. retained_variables() in declare-functions
10 Variance estimation 500 bootstrap replicate weights; Wald standard errors Wald standard errors DATA-BLOCKED. Bootstrap replicate weights are absent from the 2010 and 2014 PUMF files; Statistics Canada began releasing them with the 2015 cycle. Documented in CACHE-manifest.md and confirmed with Marc-Andre Blanchette on 2026-05-15. Not reversible without a Research Data Centre file
11 Penalty selection 5-fold CV; 10-fold CV; fixed lambda grid 5-fold CV, seed 42 Specified in Section 5.4. lasso_folds and lasso_seed in declare-globals
12 Weights in cross-validation Weighted likelihood; unweighted Weighted likelihood Section 5.4 passes survey weights to cv.glmnet. Note that folds are still drawn as though observations were independent; model-0 out4 quantified the consequence. weight_vector in tweak-data-0
One decision cannot be reversed

Decision 10 records that bootstrap variance estimation is impossible with these data. CCHS bootstrap replicate weights begin with the 2015 cycle; neither the 2010 nor the 2014 Public Use Microdata File carries them, and strata and PSU identifiers are suppressed as well. Sections 5.3, 5.5, 5.7 and 5.9 all request bootstrap intervals, and none of them can be honoured without the Research Data Centre master files.

Every interval in this report is therefore a Wald interval that treats the weighted sample as if it were a simple random sample of its effective size. It understates uncertainty. It is reported anyway because the alternative is reporting nothing, but it should not be read as the proposal’s requested quantity.

Review point 4

Read all twelve decisions. Any one of them can be overturned; the “reversal” column says what to change. This is the table to argue with.

Step 5 — The Four Specifications

Section 5.4 names four models. They are usually described as four LASSO fits, but they are not: they are two fits read at two penalties each. cv.glmnet returns an entire path, and lambda.min and lambda.1se are two points on it. Recognising this halves the computation and, more usefully, means Models 1 and 3 are guaranteed nested — a comparison that would be merely probable if they came from independent fits.

Table t4: The four specifications of Section 5.4. Models 1 and 3 draw on one cross-validated fit; Models 2 and 4 draw on the other.
Model Role Perceived health Penalty Shared CV fit Candidate variables Design columns Target (Sec 5.5)
Model 1 Primary excluded lambda.1se exclude 46 88 16
Model 2 Secondary included lambda.1se include 49 100 9
Model 3 Sensitivity excluded lambda.min exclude 46 88 32
Model 4 Sensitivity included lambda.min include 49 100 33
Review point 5

Agree or disagree that “perceived health” means the three self-perceived measures and nothing more. The ADL items and the injury indicator remain in every specification. This scope was ratified on 2026-07-29 and is decision 6.

Step 6 — Stage One, Penalised Poisson Fitting

Fit both cross-validated penalised Poisson models and persist them 
lasso_fits <- list(
  exclude = fit_lasso(design_exclude, y_outcome, weight_vector, lasso_seed),
  include = fit_lasso(design_include, y_outcome, weight_vector, lasso_seed)
)

for (fit_name in names(lasso_fits)) {
  saveRDS(lasso_fits[[fit_name]]$cv,
          paste0(fits_folder, "cv_", fit_name, "_perceived.rds"))
  saveRDS(designs[[fit_name]]$map,
          paste0(fits_folder, "map_", fit_name, "_perceived.rds"))
}

cv_curve_data <- purrr::imap_dfr(lasso_fits, function(fit, fit_name) {
  tibble::tibble(
    fit_id = fit_name,
    lambda = fit$cv$lambda,
    cv_mean = fit$cv$cvm,
    cv_low = fit$cv$cvlo,
    cv_high = fit$cv$cvup,
    n_nonzero = fit$cv$nzero
  )
}) %>%
  mutate(fit_label = ifelse(fit_id == "exclude",
                            "Perceived health excluded (Models 1 and 3)",
                            "Perceived health included (Models 2 and 4)"))

lambda_marks <- purrr::imap_dfr(lasso_fits, function(fit, fit_name) {
  tibble::tibble(
    fit_id = fit_name,
    lambda_rule = c("lambda.1se", "lambda.min"),
    lambda = c(fit$cv$lambda.1se, fit$cv$lambda.min)
  )
}) %>%
  mutate(fit_label = ifelse(fit_id == "exclude",
                            "Perceived health excluded (Models 1 and 3)",
                            "Perceived health included (Models 2 and 4)"))

path_data <- purrr::imap_dfr(lasso_fits, function(fit, fit_name) {
  as.matrix(fit$path$beta) %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("column") %>%
    tidyr::pivot_longer(-column, names_to = "step", values_to = "estimate") %>%
    mutate(
      lambda = fit$path$lambda[as.integer(sub("^s", "", step)) + 1],
      fit_id = fit_name
    ) %>%
    left_join(designs[[fit_name]]$map, by = "column")
}) %>%
  mutate(
    domain = variable_domains[variable],
    fit_label = ifelse(fit_id == "exclude",
                       "Perceived health excluded (Models 1 and 3)",
                       "Perceived health included (Models 2 and 4)")
  )

Both curves are shallow to the left of their minima. That flatness is what makes the one-standard-error rule bite: over a wide range of penalties, cross-validation genuinely cannot tell the models apart, so lambda.1se sits far from lambda.min and discards a great deal at almost no measurable cost in deviance.

Reading right to left, the order in which coefficients leave zero is the order in which the data insist on them. In both panels the last survivors are drawn from the Needs and Exposure domains; the Facilitating domain collapses early.

Review point 6

Agree or disagree with the fitting choices visible here: five folds, seed 42, survey weights passed to cv.glmnet, and the cycle indicator exempted from the penalty. Decisions 8, 11 and 12 cover these.

Step 7 — Selection Results

Table t5: Selection counts against the reproduction targets of Section 5.5. The ‘variables’ count promotes a factor whenever any of its columns survived.
Model Role Perceived health Penalty Columns offered Columns retained Variables retained Target (Sec 5.5) Gap
Model 1 Primary excluded lambda.1se 88 13 13 16 -3
Model 2 Secondary included lambda.1se 100 18 14 9 +5
Model 3 Sensitivity excluded lambda.min 88 48 39 32 +7
Model 4 Sensitivity included lambda.min 100 60 43 33 +10

The proposal anticipated 16, 9, 32 and 33 variables. Two features of the realised counts deserve attention.

First, the parsimonious specifications land near their targets while the permissive ones overshoot. That is the expected direction: lambda.min is chosen to minimise prediction error, not to be small, and the sample here is large enough that many weak signals clear the bar.

Second, and more consequentially, the ordering of Models 1 and 2 is reversed. The proposal expects that adding the perceived-health variables reduces the retained set — 9 against 16 — on the reasoning that self-rated health absorbs the signal carried by the individual conditions. That absorption does occur here, and it is visible: the exposure domain loses variables when perceived health is offered. But the three perceived-health measures themselves enter, and they more than replace what they displaced.

Graph g4 is the report’s central artifact and repays slow reading. Scanning down a column shows one specification’s whole verdict; scanning across a row shows how stable a variable’s selection is to the penalty rule and the predictor set. Variables retained in all four columns are robust. Variables appearing only in Models 3 and 4 are artifacts of a permissive penalty.

The Facilitating domain is worth a pause: it retains nothing at all under either parsimonious specification. Province, income, occupation, work schedule, smoking, physical activity, BMI — none of them survive lambda.1se. They appear only when the penalty is relaxed.

Review point 7

This is the report’s substantive output. Two questions to settle:

  1. Is the divergence from the proposal’s anticipated counts acceptable, or does it indicate that a different lambda rule, coding scheme, or candidate set was assumed when those numbers were written?
  2. Should “retained” continue to mean “at least one design column survived”? Decision 9 records the alternative — carrying only the surviving levels into stage two — which would produce smaller but harder-to-interpret models.

Step 8 — Stage Two, Negative Binomial Refitting

Each retained set is now re-estimated without penalty under a negative binomial likelihood, as Section 5.4 stage two directs. The penalty’s job was selection; it biases coefficients toward zero and must not be carried into estimation.

Comparing the LASSO coefficients in Step 7 with the rate ratios here shows the two stages doing distinct work. Sex, for instance, is retained by every specification but carries a nearly-zero penalised coefficient — it barely survived. Unpenalised, it recovers a substantial rate ratio. The penalty answered “does this variable belong?”; the refit answers “how much does it matter?”, and the answers are not the same quantity.

Three cautions about the comparison table. The pseudo-\(R^2\) values are small in absolute terms, which is unremarkable for individual-level count outcomes and should not be read as failure. AIC and BIC both favour the permissive specifications, which is what one expects when they are supersets. And the root-mean-square error moves in the opposite direction to the likelihood — richer models fit worse on the raw day scale — because a squared-error criterion on a heavily zero-inflated count is dominated by a handful of extreme observations, which the richer models chase. RMSE is reported for completeness and should be discounted here.

Review point 8

Agree or disagree that the two-stage handoff behaved correctly: all models converged, dispersion is estimated well away from the Poisson limit, and rate ratios move in plausible directions and magnitudes. Remember that these intervals are conditional on selection from the same data and are optimistic even before decision 10’s weighting caveat.

What Model 1 Settles, and What It Does Not

Settled.

  • The candidate set is fixed and documented, replacing lists that had drifted across earlier exploratory work.
  • Two variables are excluded on stated, checkable evidence about survey design rather than on analyst preference.
  • All four specifications of Section 5.4 are estimated, with both stages, and every fitted object is on disk.
  • Twelve open decisions are named, resolved, and marked for reversal.

Not settled.

  • Variance estimation. Decision 10 is data-blocked. Every interval here is Wald. Delivering Section 5.5 as specified requires Research Data Centre access.
  • Section 5.6. Cross-validated predictive performance and the C-statistic are not computed. The infrastructure is present — the folds already exist — but the metrics are out of scope for a selection report.
  • Section 5.7. Nineteen condition-specific models are not fitted. Stroke prevalence in the analytic sample is far below the threshold at which subgroup estimates are trustworthy, and that constraint should be settled before the subgroup work begins.
  • Section 5.9. Sex-stratified models are not fitted.
  • Section 5.1. Little’s MCAR test and multiple imputation are not performed; complete-case analysis stands in, with the cost measured in Steps 2 and 3.

Recommended next step. Model 1 is a demonstration that the procedure runs and a record of what it required. If the review points above are accepted, the natural successor is a clean estimation script that takes the ratified decisions as given, drops the diagnostic apparatus, and adds the Section 5.6 performance metrics — with the subgroup and stratified work handled separately, after the small-cell constraint is resolved.
